name: Atlassian (Jira, Confluence)
description: Work with Jira and Confluence from Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot through Atlassian's official Rovo MCP server: search and update work items, read and write pages, run JQL and CQL, and ask Rovo search across your Atlassian apps.
instructions:
This connector bridges the **Atlassian Rovo MCP Server**, Atlassian's official remote MCP server at `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp`. Atlassian's server provides the tools: Jira work items, boards and sprints, Confluence pages and spaces, Rovo search across Jira, Confluence and connected apps, Teamwork Graph and, where your organization has them, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket Cloud, Loom and Goals. AnythingMCP signs in with your personal API token and puts the tools behind your MCP endpoint with OAuth for Claude and ChatGPT, per-tool roles, the audit log and response mapping, next to your other systems.

**The tools come from the server.** At install AnythingMCP asks Atlassian's server which tools it offers your token, so you get exactly what your organization and token allow. Atlassian lists a small set of *primary* tools directly (`getJiraIssue`, `searchJiraIssuesUsingJql`, `createJiraIssue`, `getConfluenceContent`, `search` and a few more) and reaches the rest of its catalogue through `discover` (find an operation by describing it) and `executeRead` / `executeWrite` / `executeDestructive` (run it by name). When Atlassian adds tools or your admin enables another permission group, open the connector and click **Discover tools**.

**Setup (about 10 minutes, step 1 needs an Atlassian organization admin)**:
1. An organization admin enables API-token authentication for the MCP server: **Atlassian Administration > Rovo > Rovo MCP server settings**, turn on authentication via API token. Without it every call is refused and only OAuth clients can connect. The same settings control the permission groups; `delete_jira` and `manage_jira` are off by default.
2. Signed in as the person the AI should act as, open https://id.atlassian.com/manage-profile/security/api-tokens and choose **Create API token with scopes**. Pick the `agent-interface` scopes of the apps you want, for example `read:jira:agent-interface`, `write:jira:agent-interface`, `search:jira:agent-interface`, `read:confluence:agent-interface`, `write:confluence:agent-interface`, `search:confluence:agent-interface` and `search:rovo:agent-interface`. Copy the token: Atlassian shows it once.
3. Fill in the variables and install:
   - `ATLASSIAN_EMAIL`: the email address of the Atlassian account that owns the token.
   - `ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN`: the token from step 2, stored encrypted. AnythingMCP sends both as `Authorization: Basic base64(email:token)`, which is how Atlassian takes personal API tokens.
4. **A service account instead of a person**: an admin creates a service account and an API key with the same scopes. Atlassian takes that key as `Authorization: Bearer`, so after installing open the connector editor, change the auth type to **Bearer token** and paste the key there (the email is then not used).

**Network**: if your organization restricts access with an IP allow list, add the address AnythingMCP calls from (on AnythingMCP Cloud, ask support for the current egress IP). With API tokens the IP allow list is the only network check, because there is no OAuth redirect domain to validate.

**Safety**: every call runs with the token owner's Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket permissions, so use an account (or service account) that sees only what the AI should, and give the token only the scopes you need. Installed switched off: `executeWrite` and `executeDestructive` (Atlassian's default endpoint lists only the main tools and reaches every other operation through them, so `executeWrite` alone could merge a pull request or change permissions; turn it on when the AI should write beyond the main tools), the Jira delete tools, space and screen administration, sprint and version management, entity properties, Confluence permission, restriction, public-link and space-instruction changes, the Confluence Remix tools (15 to 30 Rovo credits each), Bitbucket merge, approve, commit and pipeline runs, Loom visibility changes and Jira Service Management alert actions. Turn any of them on per tool when you need it. Rovo `search` and the Teamwork Graph tools use up to 10 Rovo credits per call from your organization's shared pool.

**Working with it**: start with `atlassian_getAccessibleAtlassianResources`. API tokens are not bound to one site, so almost every tool needs a `cloudId`, and this call returns it for each site you can reach. Then use `atlassian_search` for questions in plain language, `atlassian_searchJiraIssuesUsingJql` or `atlassian_searchConfluence` for exact filters, and `atlassian_getJiraIssue` or `atlassian_getConfluenceContent` (with `detail` set to `full` for the body) to read one item. Not every tool works with an API token: code search, Teams and some Compass tools need OAuth 2.1, while the Jira Service Management tools work only with API tokens. A 401 means API-token authentication is off for your organization, or the email and token do not belong together; a permission or scope error on one tool means the token lacks that app's `agent-interface` scope, so create a new token with it and replace it here.

ATLASSIAN_EMAIL.label: Atlassian account email
ATLASSIAN_EMAIL.help: The email address of the Atlassian account that owns the API token (the one you sign in to Jira with).
ATLASSIAN_EMAIL.patternMessage: Enter the account email address only, for example jane.doe@example.com.

ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN.label: API token
ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN.help: Atlassian account > Security > API tokens > Create API token with scopes, with the agent-interface scopes of the apps you want.
ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN.patternMessage: Paste the API token alone (it usually starts with ATATT), without your email, spaces or a colon.

prerequisites:
- An Atlassian Cloud site with Jira and/or Confluence, and an account that can see the data the AI should work with.
- An organization admin has turned on API-token authentication for the Rovo MCP server (Atlassian Administration > Rovo > Rovo MCP server settings).
- If your organization uses an IP allow list, it includes the address AnythingMCP calls from.

tools.description: List all Atlassian sites and apps accessible to the authenticated user, including their cloudId values. Call it first: every other tool call needs a cloudId.

tools.name: atlassian_discover
tools.description: Natural-language search over the Atlassian Rovo MCP server's deferred tool catalogue. Returns potentially related tools, their tool schema and the operation names to run with executeRead, executeWrite or executeDestructive.

query.description: What you want to do, in natural language (for example "list the sprints of a board"). The server returns matching operation names and their inputs.

tools.name: atlassian_executeRead
tools.description: Execution pathway that runs a deferred read operation of the Atlassian catalogue by name (for example listJiraProjects or getConfluenceSpace). Find the name and inputs with discover first.

name.description: The exact operation name to run, as listed on Atlassian's supported tools page or returned by discover (for example "listJiraIssueComments").

cloudId.description: The cloudId of the site, a top-level argument next to name and inputs (never inside inputs). Omit it for operations that take none, such as getContentFormatGuide.

inputs.description: The operation's parameters as one flat object, with the exact parameter names from its schema (unknown names are dropped silently).
